clinicalPearls: A fat-soluble vitamin deficiency that chiefly causes a progressive neurological syndrome
Features resemble Friedreich ataxia: spinocerebellar ataxia, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, and areflexia
A pigmentary retinopathy and, in infants, haemolysis can occur
Dietary deficiency is rare; most cases result from fat malabsorption (for example cholestasis, cystic fibrosis, short bowel) or from the inherited disorder ataxia with vitamin E deficiency
Abetalipoproteinaemia is an important cause in which vitamin E cannot be transported
Serum vitamin E is measured relative to lipids, and treatment is supplementation with correction of malabsorption
reference.pathophysiology: Vitamin E (alpha-tocopherol) is a lipid-soluble antioxidant that protects cell membranes, particularly of neurons, from oxidative damage. Deficiency, usually from fat malabsorption or defective tocopherol transport, leads to oxidative injury of the large myelinated sensory neurons and spinocerebellar and posterior column pathways, producing a sensory ataxic neuropathy. Because absorption depends on normal fat digestion and lipoprotein handling, disorders of these processes, or the genetic ataxia with vitamin E deficiency, are the usual causes.
additionalInvestigations: Serum vitamin E interpreted relative to serum lipids
Assessment for fat malabsorption and its cause
Lipid profile and lipoprotein studies (for abetalipoproteinaemia)
Neurological examination and, where needed, nerve conduction studies
Genetic testing for ataxia with vitamin E deficiency in suggestive cases
reference.prognosis: Early supplementation can halt and partially reverse neurological features, but established deficits may be permanent if treatment is delayed.
pitfalls: Interpreting vitamin E levels without correcting for lipids
Missing the treatable genetic cause (ataxia with vitamin E deficiency) mimicking Friedreich ataxia
Delaying replacement until deficits are irreversible
management: Supplementation with oral alpha-tocopherol, at high doses in malabsorption, using parenteral vitamin E if oral repletion fails
Treat the underlying cause of fat malabsorption such as cholestasis, cystic fibrosis or short bowel, using water-miscible preparations
In abetalipoproteinaemia, large-dose fat-soluble vitamin supplementation alongside dietary fat restriction
Concurrent replacement of the other fat-soluble vitamins, which are often co-deficient
Early treatment to halt and partly reverse the sensory ataxic neuropathy, with physiotherapy and neuro-rehabilitation for established deficits
Monitor serum vitamin E interpreted relative to serum lipids, with periodic neurological review
Genetic testing and counselling where ataxia with vitamin E deficiency is confirmed
